comments.text_zh: 它显然不是从游戏开发中产生的。那个年代，在嵌入式或“big silicon”（amd64）上做高性能工作的许多人都完全清楚局部性、分支预测等的重要性。但游戏开发，尤其是 Mike Acton，在让这些理念被更广泛地知晓方面做得非常出色。他 2014 年的 CppCon 演讲 [0] 在我看来，是开始思考高吞吐系统性能的最易懂方式之一。就英雄人物而言，我会把 Mike Acton、Fabian Giesen [1] 和 Bruce Dawson [2] 排在名单最前面。他们都是扎实的、以性能为导向的人，都真正花时间解释他们如何思考，以及你如何也能那样思考。我很怀念能在 2013 年前后、一切还没乱套之前旁听 gamedev Twitter 的日子。[0] [VIDEO] [1] [LINK] [2] [LINK]
comments.text: It clearly didn’t come out of game dev. Many people doing high performance work on either embedded or “big silicon” (amd64) in that era were fully aware of the importance of locality, branch prediction, etc But game dev, in particular Mike Acton, did an amazing job of making it more broadly known. His CppCon talk from 2014 [0] is IMO one of the most digestible ways to start thinking about performance in high throughput systems. comments.author: yoklov
comments.story_title: Ask HN: How do I become a faster programmer?
comments.why_zh: 更多关于避免过早抽象的一种编码风格。
comments.quote_zh: 关于这种方法的更多内容，见
comments.text_zh: 我要反对这里大多数说“你没法变快”的评论，因为过去几年我明显变快了（大概快了 1.5 到 2 倍！！）。基本上，这是在我和业内同行（游戏开发）合作、看到他们产出大量高质量代码之后，做出的一次相当大的编码风格改变。我以前写代码的流程是：- 确定问题。- 找出适合这个问题的抽象。- 实现这些抽象。- 用这些抽象写代码来解决问题。现在是：- 确定问题。- 写代码来解决问题，只有在抽象确实合理、而且真的会被用到时，才把抽象抽出来。说实话，我觉得这样写出来的代码更好、更干净、也更好理解，不过它往往和某些人眼中的最佳实践不太合拍。产出的代码往往不是特别面向对象，函数往往很大，而且性能往往非常好，因为从代码写的内容到处理器实际需要执行的内容之间距离非常短。关于这种方法的更多内容，见 [0]：[LINK] [1]：[LINK] [2]：[VIDEO]
comments.text: I'm going to disagree with most of the comments here which say that you can't become faster, as I have become notably faster over the past couple of years (perhaps 1.5-2x faster!!). Basically, it was a fairly major coding style change that happened after working with others in my industry (game development) and seeing their prolific output of high quality code. My process for writing code used to be: - Identify problem. - Identify the abstractions that fit the problem - Implement those abstractions - Write code to solve problem using those abstractions. Now it is - Identify problem. - Write code to solve problem, pulling abstractions out if and only if they make sense and would actually be used . Honestly, I feel this leads to much better, cleaner and more understandable code, however, it tends not to mesh well with what some people consider best practices. The resulting code tends to not be particularly object oriented, tends to have large functions, and tends to perform very well due to having a very small distance from what the code says to what actually needs to be executed by the processor. For more on this approach, see [0]: [LINK] [1]: [LINK] [2]: [VIDEO]

comments.text: Just because it's asm doesn't mean it's fast, sure. Just because it's C doesn't mean it's faster than an implementation in your favourite scripting language. Having said that, compilers do pretty badly on C-to-simd optimisation. The best you get is loop vectorization if it's really simple logic. You can usually get some pretty good wins there. The fact you lay out your memory for simd usually is a win all of its own due to cache prefetching even if you don't actually use any simd instructions. Compilers need heuristics to manage cache when you know what you're trying to do, (eg when should it use non-temporal writes, for example?) Fast C code is written while having a really clear mental model of the underlying architecture and the assembly that the C will produce with -O3 (or whatever flag is relevant to your compiler) and then checked with -S or objdump -D, profiled with callgrind/cachegrind, perf, rdtsc etc... The compiler really can't "Do it for you" You /can/ use a compiler as one of your tools when /you/ do it. As Randy Hyde points out you can always beat the compiler because you can use its generated assembly language in every case you can't beat, so the absolute worst you get is a tie. comments.story_title: Old box, dumb code, few thousand connections, no big deal
comments.why_zh: 让你思考 cache line 和内存吞吐量。
comments.quote_zh: Mike Acton 的“Data-Oriented Design and C++”是一个很棒的演讲，能让你以这种思维方式思考
comments.text_zh: Mike Acton 的“Data-Oriented Design and C++”是一个很棒的演讲，能让你以这种思维方式思考 [VIDEO] 举个例子，如果你在检查某个对象上的一个布尔标志（1 bit），结果发生了 cache miss（而 x86_64 的 cache line 大小是 64 字节），那么你的计算机刚刚花费了从 RAM 拉取 512 bits 的全部开销，却只用了其中 1 bit。你只达到了机器可能吞吐量的 0.2%。
comments.text: A great talk which gets you thinking in this mindset is "Data-Oriented Design and C++" by Mike Acton [VIDEO] As an example, if you are checking a boolean flag (1 bit) on an object, and it ends up being a cache miss (and x86_64 cache line size is 64 bytes), then your computer just went through all the expense of pulling in 512 bits from RAM yet it only used 1 of them. You are achieving 0.2% of the machine's possible throughput.

comments.author: mtzet
comments.story_title: Ask HN: How can I learn about performance optimization?
comments.why_zh: 关于计算机性能极限的不同视角
comments.quote_zh: 如果你想理解计算机速度的极限，以及最优性能是什么样，我推荐两个演讲
comments.text_zh: 业界大多数软件慢，是因为它做了很多不该做的事。很多时候，额外的“优化”层会加入缓存，却让找到问题根源变得更难。最大的收益首先来自去掉你不需要的东西，其次才是批量处理东西。我在现实世界中做优化的套路大概是这样：1. 理解你端到端到底想计算什么。你想优化的块越大，性能提升的潜力就越大。2. 勾勒出一个最优流程会是什么样。你需要取哪些数据，需要对这些数据做什么计算，这件事需要多频繁地发生。不要试图耍小聪明做微优化或缓存计算结果。只专注于用简单的方式做你真正需要做的事。大量使用数组。3. 理解当前代码实际在做什么。你离上面的草图有多近？你是不是在计算过程中做了大量 I/O？你是不是反复回到同一份数据？如果你想理解计算机速度的极限，以及最优性能是什么样，我推荐两个与你通常听到的观点非常不同的演讲：1. Mike Acton 在 cppcon 2014 的演讲 [VIDEO] 2. Casey Muratori 关于优化种草算法的演讲 [LINK]
comments.text: Most software in the industry is slow because it's doing a lot of stuff that it shouldn't. Often times additional "optimization" layers adds caching, but makes getting to the root of the issue harder. The biggest win is primarily getting rid of things you don't need and secondarily operating on things in batch. My playbook for optimizing in the real world is something like this: 1. Understand what you're actually trying to compute end-to-end. The bigger the chunk you're trying to optimize, the greater the potential for performance. 2. Sketch out what an optimal process would look like. What data do you need to fetch, what computation do you need to do on this, how often does this need to happen. Don't try to be clever and micro-optimize or cache computations. Just focus on only doing the things you need to do in a simple way. Use arrays a lot. 3. Understand what the current code is actually doing. How close to the sketch above are you? Are you doing a lot of I/O in the middle of the computation? Do you keep coming back to the same data? If you want to understand the limits of how fast computers are, and what optimal performance looks like I'd recommend two talks that come with a very different perspective from what you usually hear: 1. Mike Acton's talk at cppcon 2014 [VIDEO] 2. Casey Muratori's talk about optimizing a grass planting algorithm [LINK]

comments.why_zh: Acton 主张把大小不一的场景图节点紧凑排布，以避免填充和缓存污染
comments.quote_zh: 当 Mike Acton 建议把不同类型的场景图节点写入 void* 时，观众席上有一个非常好笑的反应
comments.text_zh: 在老游戏里极其常见的一种做法：元素大小不一的集合类型。想象一种数组或列表，其中一些元素是 4 字节长，另一些是 6 字节。当 Mike Acton 建议把不同类型的场景图节点写入 void*，以避免不必要的填充污染数据缓存时，观众席上有一个非常好笑的反应。结尾问答环节有一个问题表达了对这种做法的厌恶，因为它用的是 void 而不是合适的类型。就性能而言，这客观上是更好的方案，但对很多人来说就是太恶心了。[VIDEO]
comments.text: Something extremely popular in older games: Collection types with non-uniform elements. Imagine a kind of array or list where some elements are 4 bytes long and some are 6 bytes. There's this really funny reaction from the audience when Mike Acton suggests writing different types of scene graph nodes to a void* to avoid unnecessary padding which would pollute the data cache. One of the Q&A questions at the end utters its distaste for it cause it's using void instead of proper types. It's the objectively better solution in terms of performance, but it's just too yuck for many people. [VIDEO]

comments.text: dyingkneepad is talking about how the cpu actually works (x86-64 & cache hierarchy). It doesn't really matter what constructs a particular programming language does or doesn't have -- we can reason about performance in terms of what x86-64 instructions the cpu ends up executing. Suppose we want to compute the sum of n scalars, represented as n 32 bit floats, say, and we're weighing up if we should store these n scalars in a linked list or an array. The "introduction to algorithms" analysis might be that both approaches require O(n) storage and O(n) running time, so they're indistinguishable, up to some constants that get absorbed into the big-oh notation. The basic big-oh analysis is true as a first cut for some theoretical simplification of a machine, but with our performance hats on, maybe we're interested in the constants being small so our code actually runs fast on a real machine -- we need to understand how a real machine works in a little bit more detail, in particular we need to have some crude mental model of the memory hierarchy. On real hardware, if we use a linked list to store our data then each node in the list may end up in an unpredictable region of memory. The CPU will need to load these fragmented chunks of memory into L1 cache memory. comments.story_title: Beyond Clean Code
comments.why_zh: 关于面向数据编程的著名演讲
comments.quote_zh: 关于它最著名的演讲大概来自 CPPCON 2014
comments.text_zh: Casey Muratori 基本上是在描述面向数据编程。关于它最著名的演讲大概来自 CPPCON 2014 [1]。我来自嵌入式背景（微控制器和裸机），所以相当认同他的论点。如果你在这行干得够久，它会显得自然又“干净”。Uncle Bob 的 Clean Code 对 Java 开发者来说大概也显得自然。就我个人而言，我最大的不满来自看到人们试图把它引入团队时的经历。不可避免地，总会有人热情高涨地尝试实现其中的某一部分，然后突然之间到处都在写一行函数。我觉得这也是 Casey 在抨击那些被搬出来的规则时，隐含地谈到的那类事情。[1] [VIDEO]
comments.text: Casey Muratori is basically describing Data Oriented Programming. Perhaps the most famous talk about it was from CPPCON 2014 [1]. I come from an embedded background (microcontrollers and bare metal) so I'm pretty sympathetic to his argument. If you work in it long enough, it feels natural and "clean". Uncle bob's Clean Code probably feels natural to Java devs. Personally, my biggest gripe comes from experiencing people trying to introduce it to a team. Inevitably someone tries to enthusiastically implement some part of it and suddenly are writing 1 line functions everywhere. I think this is the type of thing Casey is also implicitly talking about when he's railing against the rules being brought up. [1] [VIDEO]

comments.text: > Recently someone proposed this on LLVM Well, to be honest, it's not any extraordinary idea and it's not even mine. Mike Acton used this exact example in his CppCon video ( [VIDEO] at 25:58). I just happened to know that LLVM's DenseMap has this problem. On the other comment, data locality is a property (well... it's not really a binary thing (i.e, an execution has it or it doesn't), but really a spectrum; but ok, it will do) of a program. For example, a simple definition which I like is in the paper "Improving Data Locality with Loop Transformations ( [LINK] ): > Data locality is the property that references to the same memory location or adjacent locations are reused within a short period of time. Changing the the layout is just a transformation to achieve this property. So, the two things are different in the sense that one is a property while the other is a transformation, but they're not different in the sense that data layout transformations are not relevant to data locality. Regarding cache locality, that is also a property that we could define let's based on this ( [LINK] ) say as: "The property that data brought into cache should be reused as much as possible before it is replaced". Data locality depends on the hardware on which the program is executed. Since we use caches in our hardware, to have data locality you usually need to need have cache locality so these two coincide.
